transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-03
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Lopez, Samir Patel (Redwood); Lena Kim, Rajiv Menon, Tara O'Neill (NovaPay)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): okay good morning everyone, um thanks for making the time. this is our weekly poc sync, focus on throughput optimizations so we can hit the p95 latency target you shared, lena.
[00:18] Lena (NovaPay): thanks maya, yeah last week we saw the 99th really spike when concurrency went above 40, so mostly concerned about tail.
[00:27] Samir (Redwood): yeah quick recap from our side — we ran two sets: steady-state with continuous batching on, and burst tests with manual batching. continuous batching improved tokens per second by about 35% but we saw queueing at the ingress when concurrency hit higher levels.
[00:45] Rajiv (NovaPay): just to be clear, our production traffic is pretty spiky during payroll cutoffs, bursts for a few minutes can be 10x baseline. we need a safe fallback.
[00:55] Tara (NovaPay): and for the model we pinned to ggml-ish open model — sorry the name — but it's the one we tested last week, quantized 4-bit.
[01:08] Samir (Redwood): right, the quantized variant runs faster but changes the kernel selection, which affects batching efficiency. Also note our kv cache/prefix cache helps when requests share prefixes, but your workload has high entropy so cache hit was only like 12%.
[01:27] Lena: so what's the plan to reduce the p95 while keeping cost sane?
[01:31] Samir: a couple levers — one is increase concurrency with smarter queueing: set a soft concurrency target at the frontend and allow continuous batching to aggregate requests up to a max batch. second is tune batch size limits by sequence length. third is enable autoscaling with burst capacity (Dedicated) or fallback model variants for hosted.
[01:51] Rajiv: we prefer Dedicated for predictability but need to see numbers. can you show what throughput we'd expect for 50 v 100 concurrent ongoing requests?
[02:01] Samir: yeah I pulled some preliminary numbers — with continuous batching and batch size cap of 32 we saw ~14k tokens/sec on an A100-equivalent (note: kernel mismatch might change this on different GPUs). at concurrency 50 we start to see queue lengths of ~200ms, at 100 concurrency queueing grows to ~600ms causing tail latency to blow up.
[02:25] Tara: is the queueing inside the runtime or on our client side? we saw client retries which made it worse.
[02:31] Samir: mostly inside the runtime when batching waits for coalescing; but client-side retry loops exacerbate the issue. ideally set client concurrency to a target and let the server batch.
[02:42] Maya: also important to tune the request timeout and backpressure strategy. we usually recommend a token-based budget and circuit-breaker for retries so you don't amplify bursts.
[02:52] Lena: what about batching window? we tried 50ms and 100ms — 100ms gave better throughput but higher p95.
[02:59] Samir: yes exactly. 50ms window gave lower p95 but lower throughput; continuous batching is adaptive so it tries to keep window small when traffic is low and increase batching when traffic supports it. there was a transcription note — our internal doc called it continuous batching but sometimes the export calls it continuous batcher, so small name mismatch in the logs.
[03:18] Rajiv: can we do prioritized queueing? during payroll bursts we want interactive requests prioritized over bulk jobs.
[03:25] Samir: yes we support route-level priorities and token budgets; you can rate limit lower-priority traffic or route it to a cheaper quantized variant. fallback routes are a good approach: interactive -> primary model, bulk -> quantized cheaper model.
[03:39] Tara: any config for kv cache here? since cache hit is low it's not helping, should we turn it off?
[03:45] Samir: you can keep it for sessions that are conversational, but for high-entropy single-turn jobs it adds overhead. we recommended turning prefix caching off for that route or using smaller cache sizes so it doesn't bloat memory.
[03:58] Lena: about the hardware numbers — you mentioned A100 eq. if we go Dedicated, do we get the same performance on the infra you run?
[04:05] Maya: performance depends on actual GPU, MIG partitioning, and kernel sets; Samir will provide a benchmark spreadsheet with numbers across common GPUs. that should help you estimate Dedicated sizing.
[04:17] Samir: noted — i'll include batch sizes, seq lengths, tokens/sec, and tail percentiles. also will include runs with and without continuous batching.
[04:25] Rajiv: can you also add a run that simulates our production burst pattern? that 10x short spike.
[04:31] Samir: yes we can replay your traffic profile if you share it, rajiv. that will show if queueing causes p99 spikes and help us size burst capacity.
[04:39] Rajiv: i'll share the profile after the call.
[04:43] Lena: ok, pricing — maya, what's the rough delta between hosted and Dedicated pilot?
[04:48] Maya: for pilots we usually do a time-boxed Dedicated reserve with burst allowance; i'll follow up with exact numbers but expect Dedicated to be higher up-front but more predictable per-token cost at scale.
[04:59] Tara: last technical question — concurrency targets: do you have a recommended per-client concurrency setting?
[05:04] Samir: we usually recommend starting at 8-16 concurrency per client for low-latency interactive workloads, then scale up to 32-64 for batchy workloads while enabling autoscale and burst policies. for your workload, i'd start with 16 and run the client-side concurrency test.
[05:20] Lena: cool. any blockers from our side?
[05:23] Rajiv: none besides sharing traffic profile and logs — we'll get that in.
[05:27] Maya: great. recap: samir will share benchmark sheet and updated runs by 3/5; rajiv share traffic profile by 3/7; maya will send pilot pricing by 3/6; tara runs concurrency test by 3/8. schedule follow-up next week same time.
[05:43] Lena: thanks everyone.
[05:45] (call ends)
